🚀 Build with AI · Step 3 of 7 · 7 min

RAG: answers from your documents

Retrieve, then generate: the pipeline, its two ways to fail and how to tell them apart.

📚 A model has never seen your documents

What a language model knows comes from its training data, and that data ends on some date. Your internal documents, today's prices and your team's rules were never in it. If you ask about them, a model can still write a fluent answer, but a made-up one.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) works in two stages. Retrieval: a search finds the pieces of your documents that fit the question. Generation: these pieces go into the prompt, the text that is sent to the model, and the model is asked to answer from them and to say which piece it used.

The documents are prepared before any question arrives. Usually they are cut into chunks, every chunk gets an embedding, and the embeddings go into an index: a store built so that the chunks nearest to a question are found fast.

Task. In a RAG system (retrieval-augmented generation), the documents are already cut into chunks, and the embeddings of the chunks are stored in an index. A user asks a question. Put the next steps in order.

Show the solution
  1. The question is turned into an embedding
  2. The index returns the chunks most similar to the question
  3. These chunks and the question are put into the prompt
  4. The model writes an answer and says which chunks it used

Retrieve first, generate second. The question becomes an embedding, made by the same embedding model as the embeddings of the chunks, so that they can be compared. The nearest chunks go into the prompt before the language model writes anything: it sees your documents only through the prompt.

🧾 The heart of a RAG prompt

For every question, your program builds a new prompt: fixed instructions, then the retrieved chunks, then the question. Each chunk gets a number, and in the prompt it is called a source.

The first three lines below are instructions, and each has a job: to keep the model within the sources, to tell it what to do when the sources hold no answer, and to make it mark every claim with the number of its source. This number is a citation: a person can follow it and check the claim.

Answer only from the sources below.
If the answer is not in them, say that you do not know.
After every claim, give the number of its source.
[1] …text of the first chunk…
[2] …text of the second chunk…
Question: …

This lowers the risk of a made-up answer. It does not remove it: a model can still misread a source or cite the wrong one. The citations are there so that a person can check.

Task. Why does a RAG prompt say: “If the answer is not in the sources, say that you do not know”?

Show the answer

Right answer: To give the model a way out: otherwise it tends to fill the gap from memory

A model is trained to continue a text, so with no way out it tends to answer anyway, from what it learned in training. Such an answer cannot be checked against the sources. The sentence makes “I do not know” an allowed answer. It lowers the risk and does not remove it. It changes neither the search nor the length of the sources.

🔧 Two places where it breaks

When the documents are right and a RAG system still answers wrongly, the fault is usually in one of its two stages.

A retrieval failure: the chunk with the answer never reached the prompt. The model had nothing to answer from.

A generation failure: the chunk was in the prompt, but the answer ignores it, twists it or cites the wrong source. The two failures need different repairs, so always look first at what was retrieved.

Save the retrieved chunks together with every answer: without them, you cannot tell the two failures apart later.

Task. A retrieval failure or a generation failure?

Show the solution

Ask one question: did the chunk with the answer reach the prompt? If it did not, it is a retrieval failure, whatever the model wrote next. If it did, and the answer still ignores it, contradicts it or cites the wrong source, it is a generation failure.

Task. A RAG system first retrieves chunks of your documents, then a language model answers from them. One answer comes out wrong. What should you check first?

Show the answer

Right answer: Whether the chunk with the right answer was among the retrieved chunks

This one check splits the problem in two. If the chunk is missing, repair the search: the chunk size, the embedding model, a hybrid search. If it is there, repair the prompt or try another model. Temperature, model size and stricter wording cannot replace an answer that is missing from the prompt.

Task. You test the search of a RAG system on 200 questions. For 170 of them, the chunk with the answer is among the top 5 results. The share of such questions is called the hit rate. What is it, in percent?

Show the solution

170 / 200 = 0.85, that is 85%. For the other 30 questions the chunk with the answer is not in the top 5: a model that gets only these 5 results has nothing to answer from. When every question has exactly one relevant chunk, the hit rate is the same number as the average recall@5.

Task. For 85% of the questions, a RAG system retrieves the chunk that holds the answer. With that chunk in the prompt, the answer is right 90% of the time; without it, never. What share of all answers is right, in percent?

Show the solution

Only the 85% of questions that get their chunk can be answered right, and 90% of those are: 0.85 · 0.90 = 0.765, that is 76.5%. The success rates of the stages multiply, so the result is never above the weaker stage: even a perfect model could reach at most 85% here. So measure each stage and repair the weaker one first.

⚖️ The prompt, RAG, a tool or fine-tuning?

RAG is one of four common ways to give a model what it lacks. A tool call is another: the model asks your program to run a function, such as a database query, and the result is added to the prompt.

Fine-tuning means training the model further on your own examples. It changes how the model behaves: its style, its format, a narrow skill. It needs many good examples and a training run, so it is usually tried last, when the other three ways are not enough.

What the model lacksUsual choice
Small, stable knowledgePut it into the prompt
A large or fast-changing set of documents; answers that must cite sourcesRAG
Live data: items in stock, the status of an orderA tool call at question time
A style, a format, a narrow skillFine-tuning

Fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts that change: every change needs new training, and the model still cannot show a source for what it says.

Task. Which approach fits each case?

Show the solution

Small, stable knowledge fits into the prompt as it is. A large collection that keeps changing needs a search first: RAG. A number that is true only right now is fetched by a tool call. A style that is easier to show than to describe is behaviour, and behaviour is what fine-tuning changes.

Task. A shop's price list changes every day. What is the usual way to make a chatbot answer price questions with today's prices?

Show the answer

Right answer: Fetch the current prices at question time, by retrieval or a tool call, and put them into the prompt

Facts that change belong outside the model. They are fetched fresh at question time and put into the prompt, and the answer can show its source. Nightly fine-tuning is slow and costly, and a model can still mix up numbers held only in its weights. Temperature adds no knowledge, and the weights do not change during a chat.

Remember

  • RAG: first retrieve the chunks that fit the question, then let the model answer from them and cite its sources.
  • “Answer only from the sources, or say that you do not know” lowers the risk of a made-up answer. It does not remove it.
  • When an answer is wrong, look first at what was retrieved: a retrieval failure and a generation failure need different repairs.
  • The success rates of the stages multiply: 0.85 · 0.90 = 0.765. Facts that change belong in retrieval or a tool call; fine-tuning is for behaviour.
